extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers, and practitioners concerned with reasoning, scientific method, and the estimation of evidence
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles and evaluative criteria from Mill's A System of Logic about what counts as correct reasoning, the province and limits of logic, and the rules/canons for testing the sufficiency of evidence. Useful for assessing arguments, scientific inquiry, and methods of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is the science of the operations of the understanding which are subservient to the estimation of evidence; it includes both the analysis of the mental process of reasoning (science) and the rules grounded on that analysis for conducting reasoning correctly (art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill explains that logic comprises both the science (analysis of mental processes) and the art (rules for conducting reasoning), and that logic's proper province includes any intellectual operation that aids in estimating evidence. This definition justifies treating naming, classification, and definition as parts of logic because they serve the estimation of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic as the science of proof/evidence (not of belief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is not the science of Belief, but the science of Proof, or Evidence: its office is to supply a test for ascertaining whether a belief is well grounded when that belief claims to be founded on proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill repeatedly emphasizes that logic judges the sufficiency of evidence rather than producing new evidence; it gives conditions under which facts can prove other facts and teaches what makes a proof. Practical implication: when evaluating an argument, focus on whether the evidence meets logical conditions for proving the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Province of logic restricted to inference from known truths
rubrics_metrics.description: The province of logic must be restricted to that portion of our knowledge which consists of inferences from truths previously known; logic does not concern itself with truths known by immediate intuition or consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill distinguishes intuitive (consciousness) truths (e.g., bodily sensations) from inferred truths (e.g., past events, mathematical theorems). Questions about what is known intuitively belong to metaphysics, not logic. When reviewing a claim, determine whether premises are intuited or inferred—logic evaluates only the inferential step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish intuition from rapid inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Some perceptions that appear intuitive (e.g., perception of distance) may actually be very rapid inferences from experience; logic must inquire which apparent intuitions are genuine and which are inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill gives the eyesight/distance example: perceived distance is inferred from cues and muscular sensation. Reviewers should be alert to cases where something seems 'obvious' but is an inference that requires evidence/support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic judges sufficiency; it does not find evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic does not observe, invent, or discover facts; its role is to judge whether the observations and experiences reported suffice to justify conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the surgeon: the surgeon must learn facts by observation, but logic evaluates whether those observations justify the rules or conclusions. In peer review, separate methodological/data-gathering adequacy (empirical domain) from logical adequacy (argument/evidence sufficiency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of subsidiary operations (naming, definition, classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Naming, definition, and classification are operations specially instrumental to the estimation of evidence and thus fall within the province of logic, because language and conceptual organization are instruments of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues these operations help marshal facts and keep evidence/conclusions accessible in memory; reviewers should evaluate clarity of terms, soundness of definitions, and appropriateness of classifications as part of assessing inferential soundness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of rules/canons for testing sufficiency of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: On the foundation of an analysis of inference, logic should bring together or frame a set of rules or canons for testing the sufficiency of any given evidence to prove any given proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill intends a practical canon-based logic: analysis only to the degree needed to detect incorrect performance. For evaluators, apply explicit canons (e.g., how evidence supports hypotheses, controls for confounders) derived from analysis of inferential processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit analysis to what is necessary for practical detection of error
rubrics_metrics.description: The logician need not decompose mental operations into ultimate elements beyond the point at which any inaccuracy becomes visible; analyze inference only as far as required to distinguish correct from incorrect performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: in teaching bodily exercises you need only analyze motions enough to know which should or should not be performed. In peer review, focus on methodological flaws that affect correctness rather than metaphysical or ultra-fine psychological decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad conception of reasoning (includes induction as well as syllogism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning in the wide sense includes all inference (not merely syllogizing from generals to particulars); induction is as much reasoning as the demonstrations of geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill adopts the wider definition intentionally; reviewers should evaluate both deductive and inductive moves and not privilege formal syllogistic deductions over inductive generalizations and empirical inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic's limits: does not settle metaphysical ultimate facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic cannot determine ultimate questions about what is known by consciousness (e.g., existence of matter, spirit, time, space) — those belong to metaphysics and other sciences of the faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims, avoid expecting logic alone to resolve foundational metaphysical disputes; instead, evaluate whether arguments and evidence bear on the inferential claims they actually make.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science benefits from improved logical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress in difficult sciences is often preceded or accompanied by improvements in logical notions; better logic enhances the estimation of evidence and facilitates scientific advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill gives historical/epistemic rationale: clearer logical principles allow practitioners to judge evidence more accurately. For reviewers, encourage methodological improvements that clarify evidential relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic as common judge and arbiter of investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is the common judge and arbiter of all particular investigations: it points out the relations that must subsist between data and conclusions and the conditions facts must conform to in order to prove other facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication for peer review: test whether the claimed relations between data and conclusions meet the necessary logical conditions (e.g., relevance, sufficiency, non-contradiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical orientation: logic should be useful and actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: A science of logic, if it exists, must be useful; while some may reason correctly by habit, the bulk of mankind require rules laid down to guide them in inferential tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill stresses pedagogical and practical utility: logical guidance should be formulated so it can be applied by researchers and practitioners to avoid systematic inference errors. Reviewers should prefer clear, actionable methodological recommendations.
